about: HSG (Setting Scoliosis Straight) research of 2026-10-27, one agent with web search; every claim cited by URL.

hsg.summary: The Harms Study Group (HSG), run with the Setting Scoliosis Straight Foundation in San Diego, keeps the largest prospective registry of operated adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). It also keeps registries for cerebral palsy, Scheuermann's kyphosis and Marfan syndrome. The group's own chapter (Marks, Petcharaporn, Newton, Betz, Shufflebarger) settles the question the owner's letter of 2026-10-23 asked: the registry holds the radiograph images themselves, not only the numbers taken from them. "All deidentified radiographic images are obtained from the participating sites and measured centrally by trained staff", and the images are stored on a central server. The films are standing posteroanterior (PA) and lateral views. Follow-up runs at 2, 5, 10 and now 20 years after surgery. Trained central staff measure each film (more than 25 coronal and 20 lateral measures), with good to excellent inter-rater reliability. No public source says the registry keeps CT of any kind: not pre-operative, not intraoperative CT for navigation, not post-operative. So a CT and film pair from the same person cannot be expected. No source says whether the field of view reaches C2. The measures confirm only C7 to S1. Whether the image format is DICOM is also unstated. The Database User Program's terms are as the 2026-10-23 reading recorded them (USD 5,000 a year for a research tool; USD 50,000 to 150,000 for a custom research database). Today that page returned only a redirect, and nothing says whether the images come with the program. On the owner's definitions, the expected tier is gold3 for films whose field shows C2 to the sacrum and silver3 for films that show less, provided the central level reads come with the images. gold1 and gold2 are possible only if the group turns out to hold a CT of the same patient. Nothing so far shows it does.
hsg.holds:
Patients:
- The whole database holds "over 8,000 prospective and over 1,000 retrospective patients", with about 500 new patients a year across the two prospective registries, and more than 2,000 patient visits processed centrally each year (Marks et al. chapter).
- AIS registry: 4,843 operative and 483 non-operative patients in the 2016 annual report. The foundation's research page says "over 5,500 patients enrolled from 14 participating research sites".
- Cerebral palsy registry: 482 operative and 122 non-operative patients in 2016, followed for five years. The research page now says over 500 operative and over 150 non-operative patients from 12 sites.
- The HSG home page lists 37 active members and "the largest database registry for AIS"; the registry is ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01661959.

Imaging:
- Since 2001, "digital images of radiographs and clinical photographs were incorporated into the dataset".
- The sites use "radiographic digital scanning procedures and digital image acquisition ... to enable central digital radiographic measuring". In 2008 all earlier manual measurements began conversion to digital ones (HSG About Us).
- Images are acquired centrally and stored on a central server as "large high-quality image files". The format (DICOM or exported images) is not stated.
- The views are standing PA and lateral. The 2025 JBJS balance paper lists standing 2-view films at first erect, 6 months, 1, 2 and 5 years, with a subset at 10 years.
- In 2016 the participating sites had "fully integrated the EOS Imaging System", and the database was "converting from 2D to 3D reconstructions". 3D reconstructions of the PA and lateral images are pictured in the chapter.

Reader annotation:
- Trained central staff measure every film, more than 25 coronal and 20 lateral measures, with inter-rater reliability "good to excellent". Data stay unverified until checked by the QA team.
- The Lenke classification grew out of these data.
- In the 2020 JBJS touched-vertebra study, two independent examiners marked the touched vertebra on the pre-operative films of 299 patients, and the lowest instrumented vertebra was read on the post-operative films.
- The operative record holds the instrumented levels (distal level, anchor type).
- Whether the central staff store the named upper and lower end vertebrae of each curve as level names is not published.

Follow-up:
- First a 2-year study, now 5, 10 and 20 years, with a 25-year goal. 650 patients had 2- and 5-year visits in 2016.
- Studies report 282 patients at 10 or more years (Spine Deformity 2022), and 477 patients at 5 years and 84 at 10 years (JBJS 2025).

CT: none named in any source read (the chapter, the About Us page, the 2016 report, the trial listings, the research page). The CT studies of AIS that turned up in searches were other groups' work: Yahara 2019, Toyama (77 patients, T2 to L2); Queensland (low-dose CT).

Access:
- The central office handles research funding agreements and data use agreements, accepts no data without IRB approval, and takes only de-identified data.
- The Database User Program's terms are as read on 2026-10-23: USD 5,000 a year for database access and hosting, USD 50,000 to 150,000 for a custom research database. Whether images are included, and whether a non-member qualifies, is not public.
hsg.ct: None documented. No HSG source read lists CT as a collected element: not pre-operative CT, not intraoperative CT or O-arm navigation scans, not post-operative CT. The chapter names only radiographs, 3D reconstructions from biplanar films, clinical photographs and questionnaires. The trial listing (NCT01661959) mentions "3D information" but no CT. Some member sites may hold CT locally for navigation, but that is not registry data and would need each site's own agreement. Ask anyway, since a CT linked to the same patient's films is the only way to reach gold1 or gold2.
hsg.full_spine_films: Unknown per film, and it has to be checked on the images. What the measures confirm: the coronal and sagittal measures use the C7 plumb line, the central sacral vertical line and the sagittal vertical axis to the S1 endplate. So every standard film shows at least C7 to the sacrum. Long-cassette films often cut off above C7. EOS slot scans, which the sites adopted by 2016, are often taken from the skull base down, so a share of the films probably shows C2. No source states the field of view. If C2 shows: full spine (gold). If not: partial (silver).
hsg.expected_tiers:
- **gold3 (expected best tier):** films whose field shows C2 to the sacrum, with the central reads that name levels (touched vertebra, lowest and upper instrumented vertebrae, end vertebrae if stored). This is X-ray alone, annotated. EOS-era films are the likeliest to qualify.
- **silver3:** films that show only C7, or lower, to the sacrum, with the same reads. This is likely the bulk of the older long-cassette films.
- **gold4 / silver4:** the same two groups if the images come without the level reads, for example if only angle values are released and not the end-vertebra names.
- **gold1 / gold2 / silver1 / silver2:** not expected. No source shows the registry holds CT. They become possible only if the group can link a CT (pre-operative, intraoperative navigation or post-operative) to the same patient's films.
- **No tier:** if the Database User Program releases only the measurement tables without images. A table of numbers carries no image.

Caveats on level truth: a central reader's level names on a scoliosis film count from the visible ends of the field. They are reader truth only for levels inside the field, and only where the reader counted, not where the level was read from an operative note. Transitional anatomy (13 rib-bearing levels, 6 lumbar) needs C2 or C1 in the field to be settled.
what_to_ask: Whether the de-identified standing PA and lateral radiograph images on the group's central server can be released to an outside research user, and whether the Database User Program covers images or only the measurement tables.
The file format of the stored images (original DICOM or exported image files), and whether the pixel spacing or calibration is kept with each image.

The field of view of the films, site by site: whether they include the whole cervical spine up to C2 and the sacrum and pelvis, and which sites and years use EOS biplanar imaging rather than long-cassette films.
The counts: patients and films for each registry, by time point (pre-operative, first erect, 6 months, 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 years), by site and by imaging device.

Whether the central measurement staff record the vertebral levels by name on each film (the upper and lower end vertebrae and apex of each curve, the stable and last touched vertebrae, the upper and lowest instrumented vertebrae), and a copy of the data dictionary listing every radiographic field.
Whether readers record the number of rib-bearing and lumbar vertebrae, or any transitional vertebra at the thoracolumbar or lumbosacral junction.

Whether any CT of the same patients is held or linked: pre-operative CT, intraoperative CT used for navigation, or post-operative CT. If so, how many patients, the coverage of each scan, and whether it can be shared linked to that patient's films.
Whether the 3D reconstructions from the biplanar films are held and can be shared with the films.
Whether a small set of de-identified example cases can be reviewed first to confirm the image coverage and format.

The route for an outside investigator: the proposal or application steps, the data use agreement (to be signed through Wayne State), the fee and what it covers, the expected time to release, how the files would be transferred, and the publication and acknowledgement policy.
hsg.annotation: The reply to Michelle Marks is a follow-up in the existing thread. The letter of 2026-10-23 (spine-datasets/letters/hsg_ais_registry.md) already asked whether the radiographs can be shared and on what terms. The new requests add the field of view, the image format, the named levels, CT, counts by time point, sample cases and the access route. Avoid the words model, machine learning, AI and training, as the owner's letter rules require. The Database User Program page (https://hsg.settingscoliosisstraight.org/database-user-program/) gave only a redirect stub to the fetch tool today, so its fees could not be checked again. The figures come from the spine-datasets record of the 2026-10-23 reading. The chapter counting "over 8,000 prospective" patients is a Thieme book chapter (ISBN 9781684200566 in its image paths) by Marks, Petcharaporn, Newton, Betz and Shufflebarger, read on musculoskeletalkey.com, a site that reposts textbook chapters. Its exact edition and year were not found. PMC and ClinicalTrials.gov refused the fetch tool (reCAPTCHA, robots), so the trial record and some full texts went unread. Nothing was written to any repository and no grid job was run.
